text: Bread. Fuel. Something to wash with. Something to light the room. Before the Black Death, a London labourer's yearly earnings cover only about three quarters of the basic needs of a family of four. To pay for the full year's basket at that same daily rate would take roughly 333 paid working days. But the model assumes only 250 paid days in a year. That one annual wage falls short. Later, the same benchmark becomes much easier to cover. Then, the daily wage more than doubles. And the basics move further away again. How much work did an ordinary year's necessities cost? Follow the price through the centuries, and the answer takes an unexpected turn. We will stay in London and compare a labourer's daily pay with the cost of basic needs. For the later periods, we follow building labourers, whose daily wages are lower than those of skilled building craftsmen. The yardstick is a reconstructed basic budget for a man, a woman, and two children. It includes food, linen, soap, candles, and fuel with a small housing allowance. Think of an annual bill for a defined set of necessities. Divide that bill by a day's wage, and its price becomes a number of wage days. A lower number means each day's pay buys more of the basket. These are price tags expressed in wages rather than surviving records of anyone's working year. Families had different incomes and needs. Employment could be interrupted. The calculation assumes 250 paid days and adds only 5% for rent. Keep that benchmark in mind. Now, we can watch what happens when the value of a day's labour changes. Before the Black Death, the model's annual wage covers about three quarters of the basic family bill. Imagine that bill divided into four equal parts. A year's assumed earnings pay for three. One part remains unpaid. That gap is the meaning of the 333 wage days. It measures how far the daily wage falls short of supporting the model family on the assumed working year. Then, the plague changes the labour market. Population loss helps explain why real earnings improved in the following period. The struggle over wages survives in a very different kind of evidence. A law. In 1351, England's statute of labourers complains that workers are refusing service unless they receive higher pay. It tries to impose customary rates from before the plague. The text names Plowman and Shepherds, but also Carpenters, Masons and other building workers. It sets wage limits and provides penalties for disobedience. Workers who refuse the required oath or fail to keep it can face the stocks or prison. Read that as a conflict over the price of labour. The complaint comes from people trying to hold that price down. It gives us their accusation rather than a neutral account of every worker's earnings. Labor has become scarcer. Employers reaches into law. On this measure, 15th century labourer earnings are generally enough to cross above the basic needs line. The relationship between a day's work and a year's necessities has changed. For the first half of the 1500s, the London building labourer figures give us a more precise comparison. About 176 days pay for the annual basket. On the model's 250 day year, that leaves a margin above this particular bill. Move forward a century. The average daily wage, measured in silver, rises from 3.2 grams to 7.1. More than double. Before we look at prices, make a prediction. Would that year's basic basket now cost fewer days pay? Or more? More. For 1600 to 1649, the annual basket represents about 216 days pay. Roughly 40 more than in the earlier comparison. The wage has risen. But so has the bill. Across those two periods, the silver wage grows to a little over twice its earlier level. The consumer price index grows to nearly three times its earlier level. Prices have outrun pay. Think through what a doubling would do on its own. If the basket's price stayed fixed, twice the daily pay would cover it in half as many wage days. If pay and prices doubled together, the wage day cost would stay the same. Here, prices rise faster. So each day's larger payment buys a smaller share of the basket. The consequence is the extra 40 wage days. The reconstructed basket still fits within the model's annual earnings but uses up more of them. That is how a larger daily payment can accompany a tighter basic budget. Count the silver alone and the improvement looks enormous. Put the price of necessities beside it and the picture changes. Now move to the second half of the 1800s. The London building laborer figures put the annual basket at approximately 116 days pay. That is about a hundred fewer wage days than in the early 1600s. The basic bill has become smaller relative to a day's earnings. This changes the room available in the calculation. A budget swallowed by the benchmark leaves no margin within that budget for anything beyond it. When the benchmark takes a smaller share, more earnings remain outside that particular bill. That remainder could go towards more food, different housing, or other needs. It cannot automatically be counted as leisure or savings. A higher wage rate only produces earnings when the worker can obtain paid work. An actual family's bills need not match our benchmark. The 19th century figure establishes a substantial improvement on this measure. Explaining its causes would require more than these wage and basket comparisons. What they do establish is that time alone did not make the basics steadily easier to afford. Between the early 1500s and the early 1600s, the wage day cost went up. In the later 19th century comparison, it was much lower. Return to the bread, the soap, the fuel, and the light. Beside them, put a day's pay. Across the centuries, that payment grows. What changes a basic budget is how much of those necessities it can carry home.
